title: Raihan Vadra Says 74 Protest Photographs Pulled From Delhi Exhibition Hours Before Opening
excerpt: Bikaner House cited its policy and the political timing of youth-protest images in 'No Idea Is Final'; Vadra refused to remove two flag photographs and says staff removed one.
body:
• Photographer Raihan Vadra says Bikaner House in New Delhi had 74 of the 105 photographs in his solo show 'No Idea Is Final' taken down hours before the opening, after first demanding 70, then 75, be removed.
  • The removed works were street photographs of Delhi youth movements over the past year, including NEET paper-leak protests and demonstrations against the Chief Election Commissioner; the venue cited its booking policy and the political nature and timing of the images.
  • Vadra says he refused to remove two photographs of the Indian flag, and that staff removed one of them while he was away changing for the opening — he says he has video of it.
  • Bikaner House said certain photographs were 'found to be inconsistent with the policy of the Bikaner House Management Society'; Vadra says he will show the full protest collection at another venue.

An exhibition about looking at Delhi opened with most of its walls empty. Photographer Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra, said the management of Bikaner House forced the removal of 74 of 105 photographs from his solo exhibition 'No Idea Is Final' shortly before its 7 pm opening, as he detailed to PTI and as Live Mint reported. LatestLY reported the show was scheduled to run October 22 to 25 at the Centre for Contemporary Art, Bikaner House, with about 40 photographs left on display and two first-floor rooms left largely bare. He is Rajiv Gandhi's grandson and Rahul Gandhi's nephew.

What Vadra says happened, hour by hour

Vadra said the proposal was approved on June 30 last year and the layout shared a week before opening, with no objection until the final day. Twenty-four hours before the opening, management said some pictures 'might be objectionable or against their policy.' He asked for the concerns in writing. At about 12:30 pm on opening day, the Deputy Resident Commissioner called to say 70 of the 105 photographs had to go. He said he had already set aside images with overtly political slogans, and the rest had no slogans — some had political flags and a few had political leaders, which he was willing to discuss.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2113167011333419042

The demand then widened. The Principal Resident Commissioner, he said, told him the context of the protests and everything happening in Delhi was what made the artwork political. After a first removal, officials inspected and asked for more. A notice at 3:30 pm, he told ANI, said: remove them by 5 pm or the building is sealed and the exhibition is cancelled.

"When someone with power becomes afraid of the expression of another, he doesn't know it, but he has already lost the very power he is trying to protect."

— Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Congress MP, on X

What the photographs showed — and the flag dispute

Vadra told ThePrint the set documented Delhi protests over the past six months, including protests over NEET paper leaks directed at BJP leader Dharmendra Pradhan and demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar; one photograph captured his uncle Rahul Gandhi amid protests. The exhibition also included wildlife and abstract works. The sharpest dispute was over two photographs of the Indian national flag. 'They are just pictures of the Indian flag. I do not think there is anything in your policy that says photographs of the Indian flag have to be removed,' he said he told officials, demanding the order in writing. None came, he said; staff left one flag photograph in place and removed the other while he was at home changing for the opening, and he has video of the removal.

Reactions and the venue's position

Priyanka Gandhi Vadra backed her son on X: 'You stand for what is true and everything beautiful will find its way to you. I am proud of you, always will be.' Robert Vadra said his son was brave to proceed with what remained. Congress spokesperson Pawan Khera called the bare walls with exposed nails 'a chilling metaphor for censorship.' Former Rajasthan Chief Minister Ashok Gehlot called it a direct attack on democracy. Bikaner House, a heritage property run under the Rajasthan government, responded in a short statement reported by Daily Jagran: certain photographs were 'found to be inconsistent with the policy of the Bikaner House Management Society. Accordingly, their removal was requested.' LatestLY noted no fuller public explanation was available on Thursday morning.

What's next

The reduced exhibition continues at Bikaner House until October 25. Vadra says he will show the full protest collection at another venue. The unanswered question affects artists beyond this show: what the venue's policy actually prohibits, and why a proposal approved more than a year earlier drew objections only in the final 24 hours.
